extracted.intended_audience: science journalists, journal press officers, and science communicators monitoring embargo practices
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and describing embargo rules and practices used by scientific journals when issuing press releases and advance notifications, with attention to duration, timing, timezone handling, and their effects on reporting quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of short embargo
rubrics_metrics.description: For the blog author's purposes, “short” = “less than 24 hours.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author acknowledges 24 hours may be a low bar but needs a starting point for noting short embargoes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embargo duration (how long before publication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Embargoes vary from minutes to many hours; examples cited include 2 hours 26 minutes, 2 hours 41 minutes, four hours, and roughly 12 hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short durations (a few hours) are highlighted as record-breaking and notable; the post questions whether such short windows actually allow reporters to do a better job.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of embargoes (journal rationale)
rubrics_metrics.description: NEJM: the embargo “gives the media time to learn about a topic, gather relevant information, and interview authors and other experts so they can accurately report complex research findings.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also cited: another purpose is to ensure physician subscribers have the journal about the same time patients hear research through the news media. These stated rationales are used to evaluate whether an embargo length meets its intended aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum-advance press-release policy
rubrics_metrics.description: The Lancet's stated policy: “a daily press release associated with the article in question will be released at least 24 hours before online publication.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as a formal standard some journals assert; deviations from it (shorter embargoes) are called out and compared.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of embargo timing and timezone specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Embargo times must specify timezones because identical times can map to different local publication moments (example: Lancet embargo listed as minute after midnight London time vs 6:30 p.m. Eastern).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conflicting timezone information from different regional lists caused confusion; the blog notes the need to resolve which local time to follow and reports which time the journal advised (e.g., 'go with 6:30').

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency between regional/recipient communications
rubrics_metrics.description: Embargo times sent to different regional recipients may differ (UK colleagues received a different embargo time than the US press list).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inconsistency is problematic; the post records an exchange with a Lancet press officer who advised which time to use, implying journals should aim for consistent messaging across regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of press-list notification relative to embargo lift
rubrics_metrics.description: When journals email their press lists matters — examples include NEJM emailing 2 hours 34 minutes before publication and other journals sending weekly 'Publish Ahead of Print' notifications with an embargo time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notifying the press very shortly before publication is flagged as contributing to 'short embargo' concerns and may impede reporters' ability to prepare thorough coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of embargo length on reporting quality
rubrics_metrics.description: The blog questions whether very short embargoes actually let reporters 'do a better job' as journals claim, noting skepticism about four-hour (or shorter) windows being sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as an evaluative criterion: if the embargo is too short, it may fail the journal's stated goal of improving reporting accuracy and depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record/monitor short-embargo incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Track and note instances of exceptionally short embargoes as notable events (the blog posts several record-breakers and compiles examples).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The blog uses concrete examples and timestamps to document trends, implying systematic monitoring is a useful practice for accountability and discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Publish Ahead of Print' / advance notification labeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals sometimes send 'Publish Ahead of Print' notifications that include embargo information; the label and format of notification are part of how embargoes are communicated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post uses these notifications as evidence when assessing embargo length and timing; clarity and prominence of embargo details in such notices matter for reporters.
